entry.title: Why Mutable and Immutable Types Are Not Subtypes
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | crumbles.blog | discussion

Mutable and immutable types cannot share a subtype relationship without violating the Liskov Substitution Principle. An immutable type cannot be substituted for a mutable one because it lacks mutation operations, and a mutable type cannot be substituted for an immutable one because it fails to uphold the guarantee of value stability required for operations like hash consing.

Languages accommodate these distinct types through ad hoc polymorphism, such as type classes, interfaces, or traits in statically typed systems. In dynamic languages, duck typing is commonly used to allow different types to respond to similar operations, though this can complicate reasoning about type safety and data flow.

entry.title: Emulating x86-TSO Memory Models on ARM
entry.content:

Emulating the x86 Total Store Ordering (TSO) memory model on ARM’s weak memory ordering architecture creates significant performance overhead for emulation layers. The fundamental conflict between x86’s strict coherency requirements and ARM’s relaxed ordering necessitates the use of costly load-acquire and store-release instructions to ensure software behaves as expected on the target hardware.

Newer architectural extensions, specifically ARM's LRCPC (Release Consistency processor consistent) and Apple's dedicated hardware TSO mode, provide high-performance solutions for this problem. While unaligned memory accesses and older ARMv8.0-a implementations caused substantial slowdowns, these modern hardware features allow for a much more efficient transition between the two memory models.

entry.title: .tar.gz Files Cannot Be Concatenated Using Cat
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | alexwlchan.net | discussion | hacker news

The inclusion of an end-of-file (EOF) marker in the tar format prevents users from successfully concatenating .tar.gz archives using the `cat` command. While gzip is a stream compressor that allows concatenated members to be read as a single continuous stream, tar readers stop at the first EOF marker—consisting of zeroed blocks—and ignore any subsequent data.

This behavior is a legacy of tar's design for sequential access on magnetic tape. To correctly combine multiple compressed archives, the individual members must be extracted and then written into a new, single archive to ensure a single, valid EOF marker is placed at the end.

entry.title: C++26 Makes Trivial Infinite Loops Well-Defined
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | sandordargo.com | source | discussion

C++26 changes the status of trivial infinite loops, such as `while (true);`, from undefined behavior to well-defined behavior via proposal P2809R3. Previously, compilers were permitted to assume these loops would eventually terminate, which allowed them to optimize the loops away entirely. This behavior caused significant issues in embedded and kernel programming, where empty loops are often used to halt a system after a fatal error.

The standard defines a trivial infinite loop as a trivially empty iteration statement with a constant expression that evaluates to true. Under the new rules, these loops are treated as a call to `std::this_thread::yield()` to ensure forward progress. Because the proposal was also accepted as a defect report, implementations may apply this fix to earlier C++ modes as well.

entry.title: Principles for Fast Tokio Applications
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | dial9-rs.github.io | hacker news

Optimizing performance in Tokio-based asynchronous Rust applications requires balancing fairness and batching against contention and isolation. Developers should use metrics like schedule latency to distinguish actual performance bottlenecks from benign long polls that do not impact user-facing metrics.

Improving latency necessitates yielding more frequently to ensure connection fairness, whereas batching work amortizes the overhead of task spawning and runtime events. To avoid stalls, developers should minimize mutex contention, limit reliance on the global blocking pool, and isolate Tokio workers on dedicated CPU cores to prevent OS-level scheduling delays.

entry.title: Nix Binary Cache Requires Only Three Functions
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | fzakaria.com | discussion

Implementing a Nix binary cache requires satisfying only three specific requests: serving `nix-cache-info`, providing `.narinfo` metadata, and delivering the compressed archive specified in that metadata. Because the Nix client validates the archive's integrity using the hash contained in the metadata rather than the transport itself, any medium capable of fulfilling these requests can act as a remote store.

This minimal interface allows for unconventional implementations using GitHub Pages, Git's object database, DNS TXT records, and the npm registry. While using npm provides versioning through dist-tags, it lacks incremental publishing, necessitating the re-upload of entire closures for each new version.
